title: Habits (ST I-II.49–54)
hook: we become what we repeatedly do

segments.voice: Yesterday, seeing God: for Thomas, final happiness is the mind seeing what God is, face to face. Your line was made to see him. When restlessness came, did you let it stay a breath? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-eight.

At the corner of a park there's a strip of dirt cutting diagonally across the lawn. Nobody planned it. No crew laid it. It's there because people kept taking the shortcut, one pair of shoes at a time, until the grass gave up. Now it's the path. New walkers take it without thinking, because it's easier than the sidewalk. Yesterday Thomas pointed at the far horizon: made to see God. Today he comes down to the ground under our feet, and asks how a person actually gets anywhere. His answer is today's word: habitus. Or, as an old saying puts it, we become what we repeatedly do.
screen: `A DIRT PATH ACROSS THE LAWN.` → `NOBODY PLANNED IT.` → `HOW DOES A PERSON GET ANYWHERE?`

segments.voice: Thomas himself links the word habitus to habere, to have. A habit is something you come to have, a settled way of being ready to act. It isn't a single action. It's what's left in you after many actions, the worn path in the grass. Thomas says we need habits because our powers can go many ways. An eye just sees. But a will can lean toward patience or toward snapping, toward truth or toward the easy lie. Habits are what tilt those powers one way, so that the next choice comes more easily. And they're made by acts. Each act leaves a trace. Repeat it and the trace deepens. A good habit of this kind is what the tradition calls a virtue; a bad one, a vice. That's the sobering half. The hopeful half is that Thomas also says habits can weaken and fade, by not acting on them, or by acting against them. The path across the lawn grows back if people stop walking it. On Thomas's account, no one has to stay the person their worst habit made. The Letter to the Hebrews says something like this in the Douay-Rheims. The perfect, it says, are those "who by custom have their senses exercised to the discerning of good and evil." By custom. Exercised. Discernment, too, is a path walked many times. So when the Church talks about holiness, it isn't only talking about big conversions. It's talking about the ordinary repeated act, the kindness done on a tired Wednesday, that makes the next one a little easier.
screen: `HABITUS: SOMETHING YOU COME TO HAVE.` · `OUR POWERS CAN GO MANY WAYS.` · `ACTS MAKE HABITS; HABITS CAN FADE.` · `VIRTUE: A GOOD HABIT.` · then, large: `BY CUSTOM HAVE THEIR SENSES EXERCISED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick one habit to build. Settle, and breathe. Think of one small good you'd like to be easier for you a month from now. Saying thank you out loud. A pause before replying. A short prayer at a meal. Putting the phone in another room at night. Keep it tiny, small enough that you could do it today without heroics. Now picture the first step of it, in the place where it would actually happen. The kitchen. The car. The bedside. Walk it once in your mind. That's the first footprint on the path. If you pray, you can offer the habit to God before you begin. The bell holds the time.
Habitus. For Thomas, a settled readiness to act that grows from repeated acts. A good one is a virtue, a bad one a vice. Today's word.
Your line: we become our habits. Today, do your tiny habit once, on purpose, in the place you pictured. One footprint is enough. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Catholic moral teaching describes the virtues as good habits strengthened by repeated acts, and spiritual directors often suggest one small daily practice, such as an examen at night or grace at meals, to build them.

myth: for Thomas, a habit is a single action
it's what's left in you after many actions: a settled readiness to act.
Thomas says habits can weaken by not acting on them
habits fade through disuse or contrary acts, like a path that grows back.
Thomas thinks we need habits because our powers can only go one way
it's the opposite: powers like the will can go many ways, so habits tilt them.

fork.setup: you're a student of Thomas with a bad habit of snapping at people. what does his teaching on habits say about it?
options: it can weaken by not acting on it and by acting against it.
it doesn't matter: habits don't affect choices.
fork.reveal: Thomas says habits are made by acts and can fade through disuse or contrary acts. the path grows back.

original.note: Latin, the language Thomas wrote in: a settled disposition, something a person has come to have.

trapdoor: what you thought: a habit is something you do without thinking, like biting your nails.
what it means: for Thomas, a habit is a settled readiness to act, made by repeated acts, good or bad.
what a scholar hears: habits perfect powers that can go many ways; good operative habits are virtues, and they grow or fade by acts.

sources.quoted: who by custom have their senses exercised to the discerning of good and evil.

notes: All Aquinas is paraphrased. Check: Thomas's own derivation of 'habitus' from 'habere' (I-II.49.1); habits needed by powers that can be determined in many ways (I-II.49.4); habits caused by acts (I-II.51.2) and increased by acts (I-II.52.3); habits diminished or lost by cessation of acts or contrary acts (I-II.53.3); virtue as a good operative habit (I-II.55).
The index hook 'we become what we repeatedly do' is popularly attributed to Aristotle but is a modern paraphrase; the script calls it 'an old saying' and attributes it to no one.
Douay-Rheims wording to confirm: Hebrews 5:14 ('them who by custom have their senses exercised to the discerning of good and evil').
'A month from now' in the practice is an invitation, not a factual claim.
Editor: the Hebrews 5:14 lead-in now follows the Douay-Rheims ('the perfect') instead of 'mature people'; 'nobody is stuck' is framed as Thomas's account.
